name: Growth Spend and Organic Demand

positioning.oneLineSummary: Tests whether incremental growth spend preserves customer quality and unit economics or manufactures fragile revenue.
positioning.productLabel: Growth Spend and Organic Demand Lens — based on Bill Gurley's public writing
notAClaimOf: historical average CAC authorizing marginal spend

attribution.display: Based on Bill Gurley's public Above the Crowd writing

neutralParaphrase: Evaluate acquisition at the margin. As spend rises, measure whether CAC, retention, contribution, and customer mix deteriorate, and identify how much demand exists independently of discounts, subsidies, and variable marketing.

locator.value: Reasons 1-10 and lines 24-53: tactical model, spending rationalization, variable interaction, organic growth, and durability
Sections on organic demand, growth, and profitless prosperity

requiredConditions: Spend and acquisition can be observed across levels, periods, or experiments.
Customer quality can be tracked after acquisition.
Organic, referral, sales, and paid channels are defined consistently.

requiredEvidence.description: Spend, acquired customers, fully loaded CAC, conversion, and payback by incremental spend band.
Retention, contribution, support burden, fraud, refunds, expansion, and mix by acquisition source and spend band.
Direct, referral, word-of-mouth, repeat, and unpaid demand with honest attribution limits.
Mechanism that makes acquisition improve or remain defensible beyond purchasing the same media as competitors.

decisionQuestions: What happens to CAC and retention at the next spend increment?
Are lower-quality customers entering as the company scales acquisition?
How much demand remains if subsidies or paid media are reduced?
Which acquisition advantage is hard to copy?
Can the company fund payback under adverse retention and capital conditions?
positiveSignals: Marginal cohorts retain and contribute near or above prior cohorts.
Organic or referral demand grows with customer value.
Spend can be reduced without collapsing the installed base.
The acquisition mechanism has a product, distribution, data, or brand advantage.
redFlags: Average CAC is stable only because old low-cost cohorts dominate.
Discounted customers churn or cost more to serve.
Management scales spend using an uncalibrated long-duration LTV.
disconfirmingEvidence: A new channel may begin inefficiently while the company learns.
Brand investment can create delayed organic benefits that are hard to attribute.
Subsidies can rationally seed a measured network if density and retention improve.
Slower organic growth may be acceptable in enterprise markets with strong economics.
contraindications: Do not label all paid acquisition as low quality.
Do not treat unattributed demand as costless.
Do not let aggregate growth override marginal cohort evidence.

instructions: Calculate marginal CAC, payback, contribution, and retention deterministically.
Estimate organic demand with attribution uncertainty.
Test the independent acquisition advantage and downside funding need.
Conclude scalable, bounded learning, saturation risk, subsidized fragility, or insufficient.

deterministicRule.serviceBoundary: Marginal CAC, payback, contribution, retention, and spend-response curves must be computed outside the language model.

sourceReliability.high: Controlled experiments and reconciled cohort economics.

evidenceStrength.high: Repeated marginal and spend-reduction evidence supports durability.

evidenceCoverage.high: Marginal curves, customer quality, cash, advantage, and counterevidence covered.

applicabilityConfidence.high: Growth economics determine capital needs and valuation.

judgmentConfidence.high: Controlled, repeated evidence supports the conclusion.

empiricalQualifications: Short experiments may not capture delayed retention or brand effects.

rights.notes: Public author material is neutrally paraphrased.
